name: Polyquaternium-10

card.summary: Cationic cellulose polymer that coats hair in shampoos and conditioners; a background ingredient with no direct trials.
card.note: No hair-specific clinical or safety data found in the reviewed sources.

quick.overview:
Polyquaternium-10 is a modified cellulose with positive charges, used in shampoos and conditioners. Formulation literature credits cationic polymers with easier combing, smoother hair and better lather.

It is an ingredient rather than a treatment; no trials of it on hair were found.
quick.mechanism: Its positive charge attracts it to negatively charged hair, where it deposits as a thin conditioning film.
quick.risks: The reviewed sources report no specific safety findings for PQ-10 on hair or skin.

lead: Polyquaternium-10 (PQ-10) is the INCI name for quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, a cellulose-derived polymer carrying positively charged quaternary ammonium groups.[1] It belongs to the polyquaternium family, of which at least 40 members have been approved under the cosmetic naming system.[1]

It is used in shampoos and conditioners to make hair look and feel smoother. Positively charged polymers bind to hair, which carries a net negative charge when damaged, and are described as providing conditioning, smoothing, easier combing and creamier lather.[2][7] The chain is simple: the polymer deposits on the hair fibre, smooths the surface and reduces static, and the hair detangles more easily and looks neater and shinier.[7]

It is a background ingredient rather than a product people seek out by name, though it appears on ingredient lists of many hair products. Outside cosmetics it has been studied in hydrogels, drug-delivery matrices, ophthalmic formulations and sensors.[3][4][8]

chain: Cationic polymer binds to negatively charged hair
Hair combs more easily, lies flatter and looks smoother
angle.text: In shampoos and conditioners PQ-10 coats the hair fibre, which makes strands easier to comb and reduces flyaways. Users meet it as part of a conditioning formula rather than as a stand-alone treatment.

infobox: Positive charge binds to hair and skin[1]

paras: Polyquaterniums are polymers with many positively charged quaternary ammonium groups. The number after the name reflects registration order rather than chemical similarity, so neighbouring numbers can be very different structures; PQ-6 is a diallyldimethylammonium homopolymer, PQ-10 is quaternized hydroxyethyl cellulose, PQ-11 a vinylpyrrolidone copolymer and PQ-29 a modified chitosan.[1]

Research papers describe PQ-10 as a chloro-2-hydroxy-3-(trimethylamino)propyl polyethylene glycol cellulose and have studied commercial grades of different molecular mass.[9][10] Its interactions with surfactants such as sodium dodecyl sulfate, common in shampoos, have been examined in the laboratory.[11]

A 2000 review of conditioning polymers in shampoos described cationic polymers as important for conditioning and smoothing, and noted the move from 2-in-1 to 3-in-1 shampoos.[2] Their positive charge lets them bind to hair and skin and helps neutralise the negative charge on hair proteins and in shampoos.[1]

Wikipedia's article on hair conditioner explains that conditioners work by coating strands rather than repairing keratin; damaged hair carries a net negative charge, and cationic polymers such as PQ-10 help reduce static and form a light film, working alongside cationic surfactants and silicones.[7] It lists detangling, shine and static control as the main effects, and notes that some other advertised benefits are marketed more than demonstrated.[7]
Polyquaterniums are also used in hair mousses, sprays, dyes, personal lubricants and contact lens solutions.[1]

PQ-10 has been cross-linked into hydrogels characterised as pH- and ion-sensitive drug-delivery systems,[3] studied with surfactants and thickeners,[5] and used in an ionic hydrogel for flexible thermal sensors.[4] It has also been tested in ophthalmic formulations: a 2015 study reported that PQ-10 gel showed no significant cytotoxicity difference from an HPMC control in two cell lines and no significant inflammation difference in rabbits.[6] Additional papers explore antibacterial nanocomposites and 3D-printed tablet matrices.[12][13] These are not appearance applications.

Reference articles on the family do not discuss toxicity or regulatory status beyond naming.[1] A 2013 study examined IgE against quaternary ammonium ions in hairdressers and bakers, groups professionally exposed to quaternary ammonium compounds, in relation to reactions to neuromuscular blocking agents in anaesthesia; it concerned the wider compound class rather than PQ-10 specifically.[14] A 2022 study reported on adsorption of PQ-10 grades to activated sludge solids as a model of removal from domestic sewage.[15]

sections.h: How it affects the look of hair
paras: For appearance, polyquaternium-10 works on the surface of the hair fibre. Shampoo leaves hair rougher and more negatively charged, and the positively charged polymer is drawn to those sites, where it forms a thin film that smooths the cuticle, reduces static and lets strands slide past each other.[7][2] The visible results people look for are hair that detangles with less pulling, feels softer, looks shinier and has fewer flyaways, and a shampoo that produces a creamier lather.[2]

Wikipedia's conditioner article adds that conditioners coat the fibre and fill in cuticle damage rather than biologically repairing it, since the hair shaft is dead tissue; damaged, bleached or heat-styled hair carries more negative charge and so tends to attract more conditioning polymer.[7] That is the logic behind including cationic polymers in products aimed at colour-treated or frequently styled hair.

PQ-10 is one of several conditioning agents that formulators combine in a shampoo or conditioner. Hair-conditioner formulas typically pair cationic polymers with cationic surfactants, silicones, fatty alcohols, humectants and acidifiers, each contributing a different effect such as slip, shine or moisture retention.[7] The 2000 review of conditioning polymers noted the industry's move from 2-in-1 to 3-in-1 shampoos, where polymer deposition has to survive the rinsing of a detergent system.[2] Rheology work has also examined how cationic celluloses interact with surfactants and thickeners, a factor in how the finished product pours and feels.[5]

Because it is a background ingredient, consumers rarely choose PQ-10 by name. It appears on the ingredient lists of shampoos, conditioners, mousses and styling sprays and is read as a sign that a product is built to condition.[1]

The numbers in the polyquaternium naming scheme reflect the order in which ingredients were registered, not chemical similarity. PQ-6 is a diallyldimethylammonium homopolymer, PQ-10 is a cellulose derivative, PQ-11 is a vinylpyrrolidone copolymer and PQ-29 is a modified chitosan.[1] Statements about one member of the family therefore do not automatically apply to another, and readers comparing ingredient lists are looking at structurally different materials.
No studies found. A registered phase 2 trial of probiotic-containing hair products (NCT04566549, 21 participants) is not a study of PQ-10.[16]

timeline.event: A review of conditioning polymers in shampoo formulations describes the role of cationic polymers and the shift toward 3-in-1 shampoos. [2]
Research describes cross-linked cationic cellulose hydrogels, an early materials application of the polymer family. [3]
A study reports the ocular biocompatibility of a polyquaternium-10 gel in cell lines and rabbits. [6]
